title: Network+ N10-009 Study Guide 2026: Pass Free, No Signup
description: Free CompTIA Network+ N10-009 study guide for 2026. All 5 domains, exam weights, an 8-week plan, and a no-paywall practice path to pass.
author: CertQuiz Team
content:
You want a respected networking cert on your resume but don't want to drop $369 on the exam plus $40 for a VCE simulator, $300+ for a Sybex study guide bundle, or hundreds more for Boson and Kaplan practice tests. CompTIA Network+ N10-009 is the vendor-neutral networking benchmark that hiring managers actually recognize — and the path to passing it is well-mapped, even if most "study guides" online are 5,000 words of fluff stacked on three affiliate links per paragraph.

This guide is the opposite. It breaks the N10-009 down to what matters: the five exam domains and their exact weights, what each domain tests, an 8-week study plan, the free tools you actually need, and a free, no-signup, 100% private Network+ practice path you can run in your browser without paying a cent or handing over your email.

Network+ N10-009 Exam Snapshot

Before you map a study plan, get the basic facts straight. CompTIA launched the N10-009 on June 20, 2024 as the V9 revision, and it replaced the older N10-008 in late 2024. Expect it to be the active exam through roughly 2027.

DetailNetwork+ N10-009
Exam codeN10-009 (V9)
ReleasedJune 20, 2024
Estimated retirement~2027 (CompTIA usually runs an exam ~3 years)
Number of domains5
Question countUp to 90 (mix of multiple-choice and PBQs)
Length90 minutes
Passing score720 / 900
Exam cost (US)$369 retail voucher (discount vouchers exist)
PrerequisitesNone official; CompTIA recommends 9–12 months of networking experience
Validity3 years (renewable via CE credits, including by passing Security+ or CySA+)

Heads up: CompTIA confirmed Network+ N10-009 launched June 20, 2024 with the V9 objectives. Confirm with the official CompTIA Network+ page before you book your exam — pricing and retirement dates do shift.

Network+ N10-009 Domains and Weights

The N10-009 collapses the older six-domain layout into five domains, and the new weights tilt hard toward troubleshooting and implementation. If you've been studying old N10-008 material, the most painful surprise is that "Network Security" dropped from 19% to 14% — the questions there are now lighter and the troubleshooting questions got harder.

#DomainWeight
1.0Networking Concepts23%
2.0Network Implementation20%
3.0Network Operations19%
4.0Network Security14%
5.0Network Troubleshooting24%

Translation: roughly 44% of the exam is implementation + troubleshooting. If you can stand up a small network, segment it, and then methodically fix it when something breaks, you've already won half the test.

Domain 1: Networking Concepts (23%)

This is the foundation layer. CompTIA wants to know you can talk about networks without sounding like a chatbot. Key topics:

  • The OSI model (7 layers) and TCP/IP model, plus what lives at each layer.
  • Common ports and protocols: HTTP (80), HTTPS (443), SSH (22), DNS (53), DHCP (67/68), SMB (445), SNMP (161/162), RDP (3389).
  • IPv4 subnetting (CIDR, VLSM) and IPv6 (link-local, SLAAC, dual-stack).
  • Network topologies (star, mesh, hybrid), three-tier vs. spine-leaf, and SDN concepts.
  • Cloud networking models: IaaS / PaaS / SaaS, VPC peering, regions and availability zones.

Time budget: 2 weeks if subnetting is rusty, 1 week if it's not. You will be subnetting by hand. Practice until it's automatic.

Domain 2: Network Implementation (20%)

Implementation is where the exam starts to feel like a job. You're expected to choose hardware, lay out cabling, configure VLANs, and pick the right wireless standard.

  • Routing concepts: static vs. dynamic, OSPF, EIGRP, BGP basics, default routes.
  • Switching: VLANs, 802.1Q tagging, STP/RSTP, link aggregation (LACP).
  • Wireless: 802.11 a/b/g/n/ac/ax (Wi-Fi 6/6E), 2.4 vs. 5 vs. 6 GHz, WPA3.
  • Cabling: Cat 5e/6/6a/7/8, single-mode vs. multi-mode fiber, connector types (LC, SC, MTP).
  • Network appliances: firewalls, IDS/IPS, load balancers, proxy servers, VPN concentrators.

Tip: Build a small lab in Packet Tracer (free from Cisco Networking Academy) or GNS3. Twenty hours of hands-on switch and router config is worth more than any flashcard deck for this domain.

Domain 3: Network Operations (19%)

This domain is the "you actually work here" check. CompTIA wants to know you can document, monitor, and maintain a network without setting things on fire.

  • Documentation: physical and logical diagrams, IP address management (IPAM), change management.
  • Monitoring: SNMP, syslog, NetFlow / sFlow, SIEM basics, baselines and alerts.
  • High availability: load balancing, clustering, MTBF / MTTR / RPO / RTO.
  • Disaster recovery: hot, warm, and cold sites; backup types and 3-2-1 rule.
  • Network automation: scripting basics, infrastructure-as-code concepts, REST APIs.

The automation content is new in N10-009 — you won't need to write Python, but you should know what an API call looks like and why YAML matters.

Domain 4: Network Security (14%)

Security weighting dropped from N10-008, but the questions stayed teeth-y. Focus on the defense-in-depth mindset rather than memorizing every attack name.

  • Confidentiality, integrity, availability (CIA triad) applied to network design.
  • Authentication: 802.1X, RADIUS, TACACS+, multi-factor.
  • Zero trust, micro-segmentation, and least-privilege access.
  • Common attacks: on-path (MITM), DoS/DDoS, ARP spoofing, DNS poisoning, rogue DHCP.
  • Physical security: badge access, MDF/IDF security, secure cabinets.

If you plan to follow this with a free Security+ practice test next, this domain is your bridge — the topics overlap roughly 30%.

Domain 5: Network Troubleshooting (24%)

The single biggest domain. CompTIA's troubleshooting questions are scenario-heavy: a user can't print, a VLAN can't reach the gateway, a switch port is dropping packets. You need a methodology.

CompTIA's 7-step troubleshooting methodology — memorize this in order:

  1. Identify the problem.
  2. Establish a theory of probable cause.
  3. Test the theory to determine the cause.
  4. Establish a plan of action and identify potential effects.
  5. Implement the solution or escalate.
  6. Verify full system functionality and implement preventive measures.
  7. Document findings, actions, and outcomes.

Beyond the methodology, know your CLI tools cold: ping, tracert / traceroute, nslookup / dig, ipconfig / ifconfig, netstat, arp -a, route print, and nmap. Expect performance-based questions (PBQs) that drop you in a simulated terminal.

8-Week Network+ N10-009 Study Plan

WeekFocusHours
1Networking Concepts — OSI/TCP-IP, ports, protocols8–10
2Subnetting (IPv4 and IPv6) until it's reflex10–12
3Network Implementation — routing & switching10
4Cabling, wireless, network appliances + Packet Tracer lab10
5Network Operations — monitoring, documentation, HA/DR8
6Network Security — 802.1X, zero trust, common attacks8
7Troubleshooting methodology + CLI tools + PBQ drills10–12
8Full-length practice exams, weak-area cleanup, exam day prep10

That's roughly 75–85 total hours. If you already work in IT support, you can compress this to 5–6 weeks. If you're brand new, give yourself 10.

Free Network+ N10-009 Study Tools That Don't Need a Credit Card

You don't need to buy anything to pass Network+. Here's the stack we recommend, all free:

  • Professor Messer's N10-009 video course on YouTube — the gold standard. Free, ad-supported.
  • CompTIA's official N10-009 objectives PDF — download it, print it, check off every bullet as you learn it.
  • Cisco Packet Tracer (free with a Networking Academy signup) for hands-on switch/router/wireless labs.
  • Subnetting drills — subnettingpractice.com or any drill site; aim for sub-30-second answers.
  • Upload your own N10-009 question files on CertQuiz — drop a VCE, PDF, or DOCX in your browser and we'll turn it into a private quiz. No account, no upload to our servers, everything runs client-side.

Compare that to paid stacks: a Sybex study guide + practice questions bundle runs $60–$100, a Boson ExSim license is roughly $99, and a VCE Exam Simulator key is $40 — before you've spent a cent on training videos. CertQuiz exists so you don't have to.

Network+ vs Other Networking Certs

CertBest forCost (US)Difficulty
Network+ N10-009Vendor-neutral foundation, help-desk to junior network roles$369Moderate
CCNA 200-301Cisco-specific networking, deeper routing/switching$300Hard
JNCIA-JunosJuniper shops, ISPs, service-provider environments$200Moderate
AWS Cloud PractitionerCloud-first networking concepts, AWS-specific$100Easy–Moderate

Most beginners pick Network+ first because it's vendor-neutral and a recognized DoD 8570 baseline cert. If you already know you want Cisco-shop work, jump straight to CCNA — here's our take on Network+ vs CCNA: which networking cert to take first, and a deeper dive in our CCNA 200-301 study guide if you're heading that way.

Network+ N10-009 FAQ

Is Network+ N10-009 harder than N10-008?

About the same overall difficulty, but redistributed. Troubleshooting is heavier (24% vs. 22%), network security got lighter (14% vs. 19%), and there's more emphasis on cloud networking, SDN, and automation. If you've already started on N10-008 material, you don't need to scrap it — just supplement with cloud and automation videos.

How long does it take to study for Network+ N10-009?

Most people need 8–12 weeks of consistent study (about 60–100 hours total). With prior help-desk experience or A+ already in hand, 4–6 weeks is realistic. Pure beginners with no networking background should plan on 12+.

Is Network+ N10-009 worth it in 2026?

Yes, if your goal is a network technician, junior network admin, NOC, or sysadmin role. Average US base pay for Network+ holders sits in the $55,000–$78,000 range depending on source and region, and Network+ is on the DoD 8570 list for federal and contractor jobs. If your career goal is cloud or pure dev, the cert is less load-bearing — cloud certs (AWS, Azure) hit harder there.

Do I need A+ before Network+?

No. CompTIA recommends A+ as a stepping stone but doesn't require it. If you've worked in IT support for a year or two and can comfortably talk about IP addresses, DHCP, and DNS, you can go straight to Network+.

Can I retake Network+ if I fail?

Yes. CompTIA's retake policy: no waiting period after a first failure, but you must wait 14 days after a second attempt and any subsequent failures. Each retake costs the full exam fee unless you bought a discount voucher bundle.

title: CCNA 200-301 Study Guide 2026: Pass Free, No Signup
description: Free CCNA 200-301 study guide for 2026. All 6 domains, weights, an 8-week plan, and a no-paywall practice path to pass.
author: CertQuiz Team
content:
You want a Cisco cert on your resume but don't want to pay $165 for a Boson NetSim license, $40 for a VCE simulator, or another $300 to retake the exam if it goes sideways. CCNA 200-301 is the most widely recognized networking certification on the planet, and the path to passing it is well-trodden — but most "study guides" online are 5,000 words of fluff with three affiliate links per paragraph.

This guide is the opposite. It breaks the CCNA 200-301 down to what actually matters: the six exam domains and their weights, what each domain tests, an 8-week study plan, the free tools you actually need, and a free, no-signup, 100% private CCNA practice path you can run in your browser without paying a cent.

CCNA 200-301 Exam Snapshot

Before you map a study plan, you need the basic facts. Cisco consolidated nine separate CCNA tracks into a single 200-301 exam in February 2020, and the current objectives (v1.1) are valid through at least August 2026.

DetailCCNA 200-301
Exam code200-301 CCNA
Released / current versionFeb 24, 2020; v1.1 (active through at least Aug 2026)
Number of domains6
Question count~100–120
Length120 minutes
FormatMultiple-choice, drag-and-drop, simlets, simulations
Cost (US)$300 USD
Validity3 years (Continuing Education credits renew it)
PrerequisitesNone — single-exam track since 2020

Source: Cisco Learning Network CCNA Exam Topics (current as of May 2026). Cisco does not publish a fixed passing score — scaled scoring varies by question difficulty.

The 6 CCNA 200-301 Domains and Their Weights

Every question on the exam maps to one of six official domains. Memorize the weights — they tell you exactly where to spend your study time.

#DomainWeight
1.0Network Fundamentals20%
2.0Network Access20%
3.0IP Connectivity25%
4.0IP Services10%
5.0Security Fundamentals15%
6.0Automation and Programmability10%

Domains 1, 2, and 3 are 65% of your score. If you have limited study time, that is where the hours go. Don't skim the basics to chase Python and REST APIs — you will fail the exam in the simulations long before automation matters.

Domain 1: Network Fundamentals (20%)

This is the foundation everything else stacks on. If you can't subnet IPv4 in your head and recite the OSI layers in order, the rest of the exam will feel like a foreign language.

What's actually tested:

  • Roles and functions of network components — routers, L2/L3 switches, next-gen firewalls and IPS, access points, controllers (Cisco DNA Center, WLC), endpoints, servers, PoE
  • Network topology architectures: 2-tier, 3-tier, spine-leaf, WAN, SOHO, on-prem and cloud
  • Physical interfaces and cabling types — single-mode vs multimode fiber, copper, PoE
  • Issues like collisions, errors, mismatched duplex, and speed
  • TCP vs UDP behavior, when to use each
  • IPv4 addressing and subnetting (this is where most people lose points)
  • IPv6 addressing types: global unicast, unique local, link local, anycast, multicast, modified EUI-64
  • Wireless principles: nonoverlapping Wi-Fi channels, SSID, RF, encryption
  • Virtualization fundamentals (server virtualization, containers, VRFs)

How to study it: Drill IPv4 subnetting until you can answer any /XX question in under 30 seconds without a calculator. Use a free tool like the SubnettingPractice.com generator or just write 50 random questions a day for two weeks.

Domain 2: Network Access (20%)

This is the switching domain. Cisco loves it because every enterprise still runs hundreds of switches, and the exam reflects that with multiple simulation questions.

What's actually tested:

  • VLANs (normal range), trunking (802.1Q, native VLAN)
  • Interswitch connectivity, including DTP and trunk negotiation
  • Layer 2 discovery protocols: CDP and LLDP
  • EtherChannel (LACP) Layer 2/3
  • Spanning Tree Protocol concepts (Root Bridge, Root Port, Designated Port, port states, PortFast, BPDU Guard)
  • Cisco Wireless Architectures and AP modes
  • WLAN components — AP, WLC, access/trunk ports, LAG
  • WLC management access (Telnet, SSH, HTTP/HTTPS, console, TACACS+/RADIUS)
  • Configuring WLAN settings on a WLC (security, QoS, advanced settings) using the GUI

How to study it: Simulations dominate here. Build a small home lab in Cisco Packet Tracer (free with the official Cisco Networking Academy "Introduction to Packet Tracer" course). Configure VLANs, trunks, EtherChannel, and STP until you can do it without thinking.

Domain 3: IP Connectivity (25%)

The largest domain by weight. This is the routing domain — OSPF, static routes, and the routing table you'll be staring at on the exam.

What's actually tested:

  • How to interpret a routing table (routing protocol code, prefix, network mask, next hop, administrative distance, metric, gateway of last resort)
  • How a router makes a forwarding decision: longest match, administrative distance, routing protocol metric
  • Configuring and verifying IPv4 and IPv6 static routing — default route, network route, host route, floating static
  • OSPFv2 single-area: neighbor adjacencies, point-to-point, broadcast (DR/BDR selection), router ID
  • First Hop Redundancy Protocols (HSRP) at a high level

How to study it: Expect at least one full OSPF configuration simulation. Practice it until show ip ospf neighbor, show ip route, and show ip protocols output is second nature. Single-area OSPF on a 3-router triangle topology is the canonical lab — build it in Packet Tracer 10 times.

Domain 4: IP Services (10%)

Smaller domain by weight, but full of "free points" if you study the protocol cheat sheet. Lock these in early.

What's actually tested:

  • Inside-source NAT configuration (static, dynamic, PAT) and verification
  • NTP operating in client and server mode
  • DHCP and DNS — role, configuration, troubleshooting
  • SNMP (versions, function, traps)
  • Per-hop behavior for QoS: classification, marking, queuing, congestion, policing, shaping
  • Remote access: SSH (configuration, key-pair authentication)
  • TFTP / FTP function in the network

How to study it: Memorize port numbers (DHCP 67/68, DNS 53, SSH 22, NTP 123, SNMP 161/162, TFTP 69, FTP 20/21). Build a flashcard for each protocol with its purpose and default port. Easy 10% of your exam.

Domain 5: Security Fundamentals (15%)

This is the "everyone needs cyber on their resume" domain Cisco added when it consolidated CCNA tracks. It overlaps with Security+ Domain 4, so if you've already taken Security+ you can read it once and move on.

What's actually tested:

  • Key security concepts: threats, vulnerabilities, exploits, mitigation
  • Security program elements: user awareness, training, physical access
  • Local password policies, AAA, complexity, alternatives (multi-factor, certs, biometrics)
  • Access control with VLANs, ACLs, port security, DHCP snooping, dynamic ARP inspection
  • Site-to-site VPN and remote-access VPN at a conceptual level (IPsec)
  • Wireless security protocols: WPA, WPA2, WPA3
  • Configuring WLAN with WPA2 PSK on a WLC GUI

How to study it: If you have a Security+ background, this is the easiest 15% on the exam. If you don't, take the security questions seriously — ACLs especially. Our free Security+ SY0-701 practice test hits the same network-security overlap and is a fast warm-up. Note that the same wireless and ACL concepts also appear on Security+, so studying both in parallel saves prep hours.

Domain 6: Automation and Programmability (10%)

Cisco's nod to the modern network. You don't need to be a Python developer — you need to recognize syntax, understand the workflow, and know what each tool does.

What's actually tested:

  • How automation impacts network management
  • Traditional vs controller-based networking (Cisco DNA Center)
  • SDN architecture: separation of control plane and data plane, northbound vs southbound APIs
  • REST-based APIs (CRUD, HTTP verbs, data encoding)
  • Configuration management mechanisms (Puppet, Chef, Ansible) at a conceptual level
  • Interpreting JSON-encoded data

How to study it: Read 10 sample JSON blocks. Learn the four HTTP verbs (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE) and what each does in a REST call. That alone gets you 70% of the domain's points.

A Free 8-Week CCNA Study Plan

This plan assumes 8–12 hours per week and zero paid resources. Adjust based on your background.

  1. Week 1 — Domain 1 fundamentals. OSI/TCP-IP models, network components, cabling. Read Chapter 1 of any free CCNA book or watch Jeremy's IT Lab Free CCNA on YouTube (videos 1–15).
  2. Week 2 — IPv4 and IPv6 subnetting. The make-or-break skill. Subnet 50 questions a day until you can do /27, /28, /29 in under 30 seconds.
  3. Week 3 — Domain 2: switching. VLANs, trunks, EtherChannel, STP. Build a 2-switch lab in Packet Tracer. Configure each technology three times from scratch.
  4. Week 4 — Domain 3 part 1: static routing and routing tables. Build a 3-router lab. Configure static and default routes. Read every line of show ip route output until it makes sense.
  5. Week 5 — Domain 3 part 2: OSPFv2 single area. Configure neighbor adjacencies, DR/BDR election, router IDs. Expect a simulation on this on exam day.
  6. Week 6 — Domain 4: IP services and Domain 5: security fundamentals. Memorize protocol port numbers. Configure ACLs, NAT, DHCP, NTP, SSH. Skim wireless security if it's new to you.
  7. Week 7 — Domain 6: automation. JSON, REST APIs, SDN, controller-based networking. This is the lightest week.
  8. Week 8 — practice tests only. Take a full-length practice exam every 48 hours. Review every wrong answer until you understand why the correct option is correct.

For Week 8, you don't need a $40 VCE Exam Simulator. You can upload your own CCNA question banks in VCE, PDF, or DOCX format and run them as a quiz directly in your browser. Nothing leaves your device. No signup. No paywall.

Common Mistakes That Fail CCNA Candidates

  • Skipping subnetting practice. If you can't subnet fast, you will run out of time on the exam. Period.
  • Watching videos without labbing. Cisco simulations don't care if you know the theory — they want command-line muscle memory.
  • Memorizing answers from a single dump. Cisco rewords questions. Drill the concepts, not the dump.
  • Underestimating Domain 6. It's only 10%, but it's free points if you spend three hours on JSON and REST.
  • Spending money before exhausting free options. Jeremy's IT Lab plus Packet Tracer plus a free question bank is enough to pass.

Frequently Asked Questions

How hard is the CCNA 200-301 exam?

Moderately hard. The CCNA covers a wide blueprint — routing, switching, security basics, automation — with hands-on simulations. With 8–12 weeks of focused study and lab time, most candidates with some IT background pass on the first or second attempt. Cisco does not publish official pass rates.

How much does the CCNA 200-301 cost?

$300 USD as of May 2026. A retake costs another $300, and Cisco enforces a 5-day waiting period after the first failure and a 30-day wait after subsequent failures. This is why drilling free practice questions before booking the exam is the single highest-ROI activity.

Is CCNA 200-301 still relevant in 2026?

Yes. Despite the rise of cloud and SD-WAN, CCNA remains the most-recognized networking credential globally and is a hiring filter for network engineer, NOC, and junior infrastructure roles. Cisco refreshed the exam to v1.1 to include AI, automation, and modern STP topics rather than retiring it.

Should I take Network+ before CCNA?

It depends on your background. If you've never touched networking, Network+ is a gentler on-ramp at $370 and a broader vendor-neutral foundation. If you already understand subnetting and TCP/IP basics, skip Network+ and go straight to CCNA — recruiters care more about the Cisco brand for networking roles. Our Network+ vs CCNA comparison walks through the trade-offs in detail.

Can I pass CCNA without a home lab?

Yes — if you use Cisco Packet Tracer (free) or GNS3/EVE-NG. You do not need physical Cisco gear. Packet Tracer covers every command and topology in the 200-301 blueprint. Spending money on used 2901s or 2960s in 2026 is a waste unless you genuinely enjoy the hardware.

title: AZ-104 vs AZ-900: Which Azure Cert First in 2026?
description: Free 2026 comparison of AZ-104 vs AZ-900: cost, difficulty, prerequisites, and which Azure cert to take first. No paywall.
author: CertQuiz Team
content:
You want an Azure cert on your resume but don't want to waste $99 — or $165 — on the wrong exam. AZ-900 and AZ-104 sit at very different rungs of the Microsoft cert ladder, and picking the wrong one first is the most common (and most expensive) beginner mistake. Drill either exam for free in our free exam simulator — no signup, no paywall, 100% private (your answers never leave your browser).

This guide breaks down AZ-104 vs AZ-900: cost, difficulty, prerequisites, exam format, and which one you should actually take first based on your background.

AZ-104 vs AZ-900 at a Glance

Here is the side-by-side comparison most articles bury halfway down the page. Read this table first and you will know within 30 seconds which exam fits your situation.

Feature AZ-900 (Fundamentals) AZ-104 (Administrator)
LevelEntry / FoundationalAssociate / Intermediate
Cost (USD)$99$165
Duration~85 minutes~120 minutes (100 active)
Question count40-6040-60 (incl. case study)
Passing score700 / 1000700 / 1000
Hands-on labs?NoYes — case studies and scenarios
Recommended experienceNone~6 months hands-on Azure
ValidityLifetime (no renewal)1 year, free renewal online
Best forSales, PM, students, career switchersSysAdmins, DevOps, cloud engineers

Bottom line: AZ-900 is a concept exam. AZ-104 is a hands-on admin exam. They share roughly 15-20% of foundational topic overlap, but the depth, format, and audience are completely different.

What AZ-900 Actually Tests

AZ-900 is Microsoft's only Azure cert with zero recommended experience. You can pass it after a weekend of Microsoft Learn modules if you have any IT background. It covers four domains:

  • Cloud concepts (25-30%) — IaaS / PaaS / SaaS, public vs private vs hybrid, CapEx vs OpEx, shared responsibility model.
  • Azure architecture and services (35-40%) — regions, availability zones, core compute / storage / networking services, VMs, App Service, Azure SQL.
  • Azure management and governance (30-35%) — cost calculator, TCO, SLAs, Azure Policy, RBAC at a high level, Azure Portal vs CLI vs PowerShell.

You will not configure a thing on AZ-900. There are no command outputs to read, no IP subnetting, no Azure CLI flags. If a question feels too technical, it is probably a distractor.

What AZ-104 Actually Tests

AZ-104 is where Microsoft starts caring whether you have ever logged into the Azure Portal. The April 17, 2026 skills outline lists five domains:

  1. Manage Azure identities and governance (20-25%) — Microsoft Entra ID, users, groups, RBAC, Azure Policy, subscriptions, management groups.
  2. Implement and manage storage (15-20%) — storage accounts, blob lifecycle, Azure Files, AzCopy, access tiers, redundancy options.
  3. Deploy and manage Azure compute resources (20-25%) — VMs, scale sets, ARM templates, Bicep, App Service, container instances, AKS basics.
  4. Implement and manage virtual networking (15-20%) — VNets, subnets, NSGs, peering, VPN gateway, Load Balancer, App Gateway, DNS.
  5. Monitor and maintain Azure resources (10-15%) — Azure Monitor, Log Analytics, alerts, backup, Site Recovery, update management.

Expect a case study with 4-6 linked questions, drag-and-drop ordering, and PowerShell / Azure CLI snippets where you pick the missing parameter. Roughly 30-40% of AZ-104 questions assume you have actually clicked through the Portal — reading-only prep does not work here.

Cost: AZ-900 First Can Save You $165

Microsoft retake fees are brutal. If you fail AZ-104 cold, you pay $165 again, plus a 24-hour wait before retest 1 and a 14-day wait before retest 2. That is why the cheap path is rarely the cheap path.

Path Total cost if you pass first try Total cost if you fail AZ-104 once
AZ-104 only$165$330
AZ-900 then AZ-104$264$429
AZ-900 then AZ-104 (and AZ-900 lifts AZ-104 pass rate)$264Most candidates avoid the retake entirely

For under-$100 insurance against a $165 retake, AZ-900 first is a no-brainer for most beginners. The only people who should skip AZ-900 are working sysadmins with 6+ months of real Azure Portal experience.

Difficulty: How the Two Exams Feel in the Room

Real candidate reports converge on a clear pattern. AZ-900 feels like a written quiz: read, recognize, click. AZ-104 feels like a workday simulation: read a 5-paragraph scenario, eliminate two obviously wrong options, then sweat between the last two.

The biggest jump is not the volume of facts — it is the question style. AZ-104 weaponizes the “most appropriate” phrasing. Two answers will technically work; only one is the cheapest, fastest, or most aligned with Microsoft best practice. If you have only watched videos, you will not feel the difference between the two.

Plan for at least 80-120 hours of study for AZ-104 if you have AZ-900 already, or 150-200 hours if you are starting cold. AZ-900 is a 20-40 hour exam for most people with any IT background.

Career Value: Which Cert Actually Gets You Hired?

AZ-900 alone will not get you an Azure job. Recruiters use it as a tiebreaker between two otherwise-similar resumes, or as proof that a non-technical PM understands cloud terminology. AZ-104 is the cert that opens cloud-administrator job listings — recruiters search for it by name.

Which Should You Take First? A 30-Second Decision Rule

Use this flowchart with no hedging:

  • Have you used the Azure Portal for < 50 hours? → AZ-900 first.
  • Are you in a non-technical role (PM, sales, marketing)? → AZ-900, and stop there.
  • Are you a working Windows / Linux sysadmin with 6+ months Azure exposure? → Skip to AZ-104.
  • Do you want to add Azure to a CCNA or Security+? → AZ-900 first — concepts overlap with cloud security questions on your other certs.
  • Is your employer reimbursing only one exam? → AZ-104 — higher resume value per dollar.

Microsoft Learn covers ~80% of both objective lists for free. The other 20% — the timing, the question phrasing, the case-study pacing — you only get from drilling actual questions. Paid simulators like MeasureUp, Whizlabs, and Kaplan run $30-$80 per exam.

You do not need them. Here is the free path:

  2. Get a free Azure account and click through the Portal for 5-10 hours. Build a VM, create a storage account, set an NSG rule.

Is AZ-900 required before AZ-104?

No. Microsoft does not require AZ-900 as a prerequisite for AZ-104. You can register for and pass AZ-104 without ever taking AZ-900. Microsoft does, however, recommend at least 6 months of hands-on Azure experience before AZ-104, so most beginners take AZ-900 first as a low-cost stepping stone.

How much harder is AZ-104 than AZ-900?

Roughly 3 to 4 times harder for someone with no hands-on Azure experience. AZ-900 is a concept-recognition exam — if you can define a load balancer, you can pass. AZ-104 expects you to configure one. Most candidates report needing 80-150 more study hours for AZ-104 than for AZ-900.

Does AZ-900 expire?

No. AZ-900 is one of the few Microsoft certs with lifetime validity — once you pass it, it stays on your transcript. AZ-104 expires one year after passing, but Microsoft renews it for free with an open-book online assessment, so it never costs you another $165 unless you let it lapse.

Yes, with a caveat. AWS CCP and AZ-900 cover ~60% identical concepts (cloud models, shared responsibility, OpEx vs CapEx). If you scored well on CCP, you do not need AZ-900 to function on AZ-104 — but Azure-specific service names, pricing tiers, and governance tools (Azure Policy, Entra ID, Resource Manager) will still trip you up. Budget 10-15 hours of Azure-specific study before AZ-104, even with CCP in hand.

title: Security+ SY0-701 Domains Explained: 2026 Breakdown
description: Free 2026 breakdown of all 5 CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 domains, weights, and what to study first. No paywall, no signup.
author: CertQuiz Team
content:
If you're studying for the CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 and you don't know exactly how the five domains are weighted, you're studying blind. CompTIA tells you what to study, but not where the points are — and the points cluster heavily in just three domains.

This guide breaks down all five SY0-701 domains, what each one covers, the exact percentage of the exam each represents, and which one to study first. Then it points you at a free, no-signup, 100% private SY0-701 practice test you can run in your browser without paying $40 for a simulator.

The 5 SY0-701 Domains at a Glance

CompTIA released SY0-701 in November 2023, restructuring the old SY0-601 from six domains down to five and shifting weight toward operations and governance. These are the current domains as of the 2026 objectives:

#DomainWeight
1General Security Concepts12%
2Threats, Vulnerabilities, and Mitigations22%
3Security Architecture18%
4Security Operations28%
5Security Program Management and Oversight20%

Source: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Exam Objectives (Version 5.0, current as of May 2026).

Domains 2, 4, and 5 are 70% of the exam. Domain 4 alone is more than a quarter of your score. If you have limited study time, that's where it goes — not into memorizing every CIA Triad acronym.

Domain 1: General Security Concepts (12%)

This is the smallest domain by weight, but it sets the vocabulary for everything else. Skip it and the other four domains will feel like a foreign language.

What's actually tested:

  • Security control categories (technical, managerial, operational, physical) and types (preventive, deterrent, detective, corrective, compensating, directive)
  • The CIA triad — confidentiality, integrity, availability — plus non-repudiation and AAA (authentication, authorization, accounting)
  • Zero Trust principles and the policy/data planes
  • Cryptographic concepts: PKI, symmetric vs asymmetric, hashing, digital signatures, key escrow, salting
  • Change management processes — approval, ownership, stakeholders, impact analysis, test results, backout plans

How to study it: Learn the definitions cold, but spend more time on Zero Trust and PKI — those concepts repeat all over Domains 3, 4, and 5.

Domain 2: Threats, Vulnerabilities, and Mitigations (22%)

Most candidates' favorite domain because it's the closest to "real cybersecurity." It is also the second-heaviest on the exam.

What's actually tested:

  • Threat actors — nation-state, unskilled, hacktivist, insider threat, organized crime, shadow IT — and their motivations
  • Threat vectors and attack surfaces: messages, images, files, voice calls, removable devices, vulnerable software, unsupported systems
  • Specific attack types: malware (ransomware, trojan, worm, spyware, bloatware, virus, keylogger, logic bomb, rootkit), social engineering (phishing, vishing, smishing, BEC, pretexting), application attacks (injection, buffer overflow, race conditions, XSS), cryptographic attacks, password attacks
  • Indicators of compromise and how to spot them
  • Mitigation techniques — segmentation, isolation, patching, encryption, monitoring, hardening, configuration enforcement, decommissioning

How to study it: Make a flashcard for every named attack and threat actor. Then for each, write a one-line "what it looks like in a SOC alert" note. PBQs in this domain often show you a packet capture or log snippet and ask you to name the attack.

Domain 3: Security Architecture (18%)

Many test-takers cite this as the hardest domain. It's heavy on cloud, hybrid, and on-prem design choices, plus identity and resilience patterns. There's no single right answer for many questions — you have to weigh trade-offs.

What's actually tested:

  • Architecture models — cloud, IaC, serverless, microservices, network architecture (physical/logical, SDN), on-premises vs hybrid, containerization, virtualization, IoT, ICS/SCADA, embedded systems
  • Securing enterprise infrastructure: ports, protocols, firewalls (WAF, NGFW, UTM), IDS/IPS, secure access service edge (SASE), VPNs, jump servers, proxy servers, load balancers
  • Data protection — classification, encryption at rest/in transit/in use, hashing, masking, tokenization, obfuscation, segmentation
  • Resilience and recovery — high availability, site resilience (hot/warm/cold), platform diversity, multi-cloud, capacity planning, testing (parallel, simulation, tabletop, failover), backups, power redundancy

How to study it: Draw network diagrams. Sketch the difference between a hot site and a warm site. Diagram a hub-and-spoke versus a SASE deployment. The exam loves architecture trade-off questions, and you can't reason about a topology if you've only ever read about it.

Domain 4: Security Operations (28%)

The biggest domain, the most performance-based questions (PBQs), and the toughest one for new IT entrants. Roughly 28% of your exam is here, so this is where the bulk of your study hours should land.

What's actually tested:

  • Common security techniques: secure baselines, hardening (mobile, workstations, switches, routers, cloud, servers, ICS, IoT, embedded), wireless settings (WPA3, AAA/RADIUS, 802.1X)
  • Asset, vulnerability, and patch management — the full lifecycle from acquisition to decommissioning
  • Vulnerability scanning, CVSS, CVE, validation, prioritization, and remediation
  • Monitoring tooling — SIEM, agents, NetFlow, vulnerability scanners, SCAP, antivirus/DLP/SNMP traps, log aggregation
  • Identity and access management — provisioning, de-provisioning, federation, SSO (SAML, OAuth, OIDC), interoperability, attestation, MFA, password concepts (length, complexity, age, reuse, expiration), privileged access management (PAM, just-in-time)
  • Automation and orchestration (SOAR), scripting use cases, EDR/XDR
  • Incident response — preparation, detection, analysis, containment, eradication, recovery, lessons learned, plus root cause analysis, threat hunting, and digital forensics (legal hold, chain of custody, acquisition, reporting, preservation, e-discovery)

How to study it: Plan to spend two to three weeks on Domain 4 alone. Use scenario-based practice questions, not flashcards. The PBQs in your real exam almost always come from this domain — typically log analysis, configuring a firewall ruleset, or walking an incident response.

Domain 5: Security Program Management and Oversight (20%)

Often dismissed as "the boring governance domain." It is also a fifth of your score. Underestimate it and you'll fail.

What's actually tested:

  • Effective security governance — policies, standards, procedures, guidelines, regulatory considerations, governance structures (boards, committees, government entities)
  • Risk management process — identification, assessment (qualitative, quantitative, ad hoc, recurring), analysis (likelihood, impact, ALE/ARO/SLE), risk register, KRIs, risk appetite, exception/exemption handling, risk treatment options
  • Third-party risk — vendor assessment, supply chain analysis, due diligence, contracts (SLA, MOA, MOU, NDA, BPA), questionnaires, rules of engagement
  • Compliance — reporting, monitoring, consequences (fines, sanctions, reputational, loss of license), privacy (GDPR, controllers, processors, data subjects, retention)
  • Audits and assessments — internal, external, penetration testing (physical, offensive, defensive, integrated, known/partially known/unknown environment), reconnaissance
  • Security awareness — phishing campaigns, training, recognition for reporting, anomalous behavior recognition, user guidance, role-based training

How to study it: Memorize formulas (SLE = Asset Value × Exposure Factor; ALE = SLE × ARO). Memorize the contract acronyms. The exam tests this domain with crisp definitional questions, so it's the easiest 20% of the test if you put in the time.

Recommended Study Order

Don't study the domains in the order CompTIA lists them, and don't study them equally. Use this order instead:

  1. Week 1 — Domain 1. Build the vocabulary. Skim once, take notes, move on.
  2. Week 2 — Domain 2. Threats and attacks. Most fun, builds momentum.
  3. Week 3 — Domain 5. Governance, risk, and compliance. Knock out the formulas and contracts while your brain is fresh.
  4. Weeks 4-5 — Domain 4. The biggest and hardest. Two weeks minimum, with hands-on practice in a free SIEM (Wazuh or Security Onion) and a vulnerability scanner (OpenVAS, Nessus Essentials).
  5. Week 6 — Domain 3. Architecture, design, and trade-offs. Easier once you've seen the operational tools first.
  6. Weeks 7-8 — Practice tests and PBQs only. Stop reading. Start drilling.

For Weeks 7-8, you don't need a $40 VCE Exam Simulator. You can take our free Security+ SY0-701 practice test in your browser, or upload your own SY0-701 question banks in VCE, PDF, or DOCX format. Nothing leaves your device. No signup. No paywall.

SY0-701 Exam Snapshot

DetailSY0-701
Number of domains5
Maximum questions90
Length90 minutes
FormatMultiple-choice, multiple-response, performance-based
Passing score750 out of 900 (scaled)
Cost (US)$425 USD voucher
Validity3 years (CEUs renew it)
ReleasedNovember 2023; current objectives Version 5.0

Source: CompTIA Security+ official page and the SY0-701 Exam Objectives PDF (Version 5.0, current as of May 2026).

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the hardest domain on the SY0-701?

Most candidates name Domain 4 (Security Operations) or Domain 3 (Security Architecture). Domain 4 is hardest by sheer volume — at 28% of the exam, it carries the most performance-based questions and the most operational depth. Domain 3 is hardest conceptually because it asks for trade-off reasoning across cloud, hybrid, and on-prem architectures with no single right answer.

How many domains does the Security+ SY0-701 have?

Five. CompTIA cut the previous SY0-601 from six domains down to five when SY0-701 launched in November 2023, consolidating identity content into Security Operations and beefing up governance into its own dedicated domain.

Which SY0-701 domain should I study first?

Start with Domain 1 (General Security Concepts). It's the smallest at 12%, but it defines the vocabulary — controls, the CIA triad, AAA, Zero Trust, PKI — that every other domain reuses. Skipping it means re-learning the same terms three more times. See our full Security+ study guide for a week-by-week plan.

How is the SY0-701 scored?

The exam uses a scaled score of 100 to 900, with a passing score of 750. Performance-based questions (PBQs) are weighted more heavily than standard multiple-choice questions. CompTIA does not publish per-question weights or domain-level subscores, so a strong showing in Domain 4 can offset weakness in Domain 1.

Are the SY0-701 domain weights changing in 2026?

No. Version 5.0 of the SY0-701 objectives is current as of May 2026, with the same five domains and the same 12 / 22 / 18 / 28 / 20 weighting. CompTIA typically releases a new exam version (SY0-801, etc.) every three years, so SY0-701 should remain the active exam through at least mid-to-late 2026. title: AZ-900 Azure Fundamentals Study Guide 2026: Pass Free

The Microsoft Azure Fundamentals (AZ-900) exam is the cheapest, fastest way to put a Microsoft cloud credential on your resume. It is 45 minutes long, costs $99, and most candidates pass with two to four weeks of casual study.

This guide gives you the full AZ-900 blueprint, the services Microsoft actually tests, a free 3-week study plan, and a free, no-signup, 100% private practice test path you can start in under a minute.

What Is the AZ-900 Azure Fundamentals Exam?

AZ-900 is the entry-level Microsoft certification for anyone — technical or not — who needs to demonstrate baseline Azure fluency. Microsoft positions it for sales, project managers, recruiters, and IT staff getting their first cloud credential. It is entirely conceptual: you will never be asked to configure a virtual machine inside the Azure portal.

The 3 AZ-900 Exam Domains (and Their Weights)

Every question on the exam maps to one of three domains. Memorize the weights — they tell you where to spend your study time.

#DomainWeight
1Describe Cloud Concepts25-30%
2Describe Azure Architecture and Services35-40%
3Describe Azure Management and Governance30-35%

Domain 2 plus Domain 3 are at least 65% of your score. If you only have a weekend, that is where to focus.

Domain 1: Describe Cloud Concepts (25-30%)

The "why cloud?" domain. Expect questions on the cloud value proposition (high availability, scalability, elasticity, reliability, predictability, security, governance, manageability), CapEx vs OpEx, the consumption-based pricing model, and the differences between IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS service models. Public, private, and hybrid cloud deployment models are also tested here.

Domain 2: Describe Azure Architecture and Services (35-40%)

The largest and most-tested domain. You need to recognize Azure's core architectural components — regions, region pairs, availability zones, resource groups, subscriptions, management groups, and Azure Resource Manager (ARM). On the services side, focus on compute (Virtual Machines, App Service, Container Instances, AKS, Azure Functions), networking (Virtual Network, VPN Gateway, ExpressRoute, DNS), storage (Blob, Disk, File, Queue, Table), and database services (Cosmos DB, Azure SQL, Database for MySQL/PostgreSQL).

Domain 3: Describe Azure Management and Governance (30-35%)

The domain that changed most in the January 2026 refresh. Cost management is now front and center: the Azure Pricing Calculator, the Total Cost of Ownership (TCO) Calculator, Microsoft Cost Management, and Azure Reservations. Then come governance and compliance tools — Azure Policy, role-based access control (RBAC), resource locks, tagging, and Microsoft Purview for compliance and data governance. Finally, the monitoring stack: Azure Monitor, Azure Service Health, and Azure Advisor.

Core Azure Services You Must Know

The AZ-900 covers dozens of services at a surface level, but most questions cluster around the same 25 or so. Lock these in first:

  • Compute: Virtual Machines, Virtual Machine Scale Sets, App Service, Container Instances, Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS), Azure Functions, Azure Virtual Desktop
  • Networking: Virtual Network (VNet), Subnets, VPN Gateway, ExpressRoute, Azure DNS, Azure Load Balancer, Application Gateway
  • Storage: Blob Storage (and access tiers), Disk Storage, File Storage, Queue Storage, Table Storage, Azure Storage Explorer
  • Database: Azure SQL Database, Azure SQL Managed Instance, Cosmos DB, Database for MySQL/PostgreSQL
  • Identity & Security: Microsoft Entra ID (formerly Azure AD), Multi-Factor Authentication, Conditional Access, RBAC, Microsoft Defender for Cloud, Azure Key Vault
  • Management & Monitoring: Azure Monitor, Azure Advisor, Azure Service Health, Azure Resource Manager, Azure Policy, Microsoft Cost Management, Microsoft Purview
  • Migration & Cost: Azure Migrate, Azure Data Box, Pricing Calculator, TCO Calculator, Azure Reservations

A Free 3-Week Study Plan

This plan assumes ~8 hours per week and zero paid resources.

  1. Week 1 — Foundations. Complete the official Microsoft Learn AZ-900 learning paths (free, ~14 hours). They map exactly to the exam objectives. Skim the official Microsoft AZ-900 study guide PDF end to end so you know what is in scope and what is not.
  2. Week 2 — Hands-on + Domains 2 & 3. Sign up for an Azure Free Account (12 months of select services + $200 credit). Spin up a VM, create a storage account, set up a resource group, attach a tag, then tear it all down. Concept questions get easier once you've clicked the buttons once. Drill service one-liners with flashcards (Anki or a free Quizlet deck).
  3. Week 3 — Practice tests only. Take a full-length practice exam every other day. Review every wrong answer until you understand why the correct option is correct. Stop when you score 80%+ on two practice exams in a row.

For Week 3, you don't need a $40 simulator. You can upload your own AZ-900 question banks in VCE, PDF, or DOCX format and run them as a quiz directly in your browser. No signup, nothing uploaded to a server, 100% private.

Common Mistakes That Fail Candidates

  • Memorizing services without understanding use cases. The exam asks "which service fits this scenario," not "define App Service."
  • Confusing IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS. Know the line of responsibility. With IaaS you patch the OS; with PaaS Microsoft does. SaaS is fully managed for you.
  • Skipping cost management tools. The Pricing Calculator vs the TCO Calculator vs Microsoft Cost Management — easy points if you know the difference, easy losses if you don't.
  • Cramming with no practice tests. AZ-900 questions are scenario-based, not vocab quizzes. You need to see the format before exam day.
  • Ignoring the January 2026 refresh. Microsoft Purview, the renamed Microsoft Entra ID (formerly Azure AD), and the restructured governance section all matter on the current exam.

How hard is the AZ-900 Azure Fundamentals exam?

Compared to other IT certifications, it is on the easy side. Reported first-attempt pass rates sit around 70-75%, slightly higher than AWS Cloud Practitioner. With 30-50 hours of focused study and a few practice tests, most beginners pass on the first attempt. Don't mistake "easier than CCNA" for "trivial," though — the breadth of Azure services still surprises non-technical candidates.

How much does the AZ-900 exam cost in 2026?

$99 USD in the United States. Pricing varies by region (around ₹3,691 in India, for example). Microsoft occasionally releases free voucher promotions through events like Microsoft Ignite or the Cloud Skills Challenge — check the Microsoft Learn site before you book.

Is AZ-900 worth it in 2026?

Yes for non-engineers (sales, project managers, recruiters, students) who need cloud fluency on their resume.   2. Week 2 — Hands-on + Domains 1 & 2. Open an AWS Free Tier account. Spin up an EC2 instance, create an S3 bucket, attach an IAM policy, then tear it all down. Concept questions get easier once you've clicked the buttons once.
  3. Week 3 — Domains 3 & 4. Memorize service one-liners. Drill pricing models and Support plans with flashcards (Anki, or a free Quizlet deck).
  4. Week 4 — Practice tests only. Take a full-length practice exam every other day. Review every wrong answer until you understand why the correct option is correct. Stop when you score 80%+ on two practice exams in a row.

It is moderately difficult — broad rather than deep. Reported pass rates hover around 70%. With 30–60 hours of focused study and a few practice tests, most beginners pass on the first attempt.

title: CompTIA A+ vs Network+: Which Certification Should You Get First? (2026)
description: CompTIA A+ vs Network+ compared with salary data, exam difficulty, pass rates, and job market stats. Free 2026 guide to choosing the right entry-level IT certification for your career.
author: CertQuiz Team
content:
CompTIA A+ and CompTIA Network+ are the two most popular entry-level IT certifications in the world. Both are CompTIA credentials. Both appear on hiring managers’ wish lists. But they test completely different skill sets — and choosing the wrong one first can mean months of misdirected study and a certification that doesn’t match the jobs you’re actually applying for.

The short answer: A+ is the broader entry point for IT support and help desk roles; Network+ is a more focused networking credential that commands higher average pay. This guide breaks down the real differences using current salary figures, exam details, and job market data. Already studying? Upload your practice exam files to our free browser-based simulator and start testing today — no signup required.

Key Takeaways

  • A+ holders earn a median ~$54K–$64K/yr in help desk and support roles; Network+ holders average ~$74K–$82K/yr in networking positions (ZipRecruiter / PayScale, 2025)
  • A+ requires passing two separate exams (Core 1 + Core 2) at ~$246 each (~$492 total); Network+ is a single $369 exam
  • Both exams have an estimated 70–80% first-attempt pass rate, making them more accessible than Cisco CCNA (~50–60%)
  • Demand for computer support specialists is projected to grow 6% through 2033, faster than the average for all occupations (BLS, 2024)
  • Best path: Start with A+ if you have no IT background and want help desk work; start with Network+ if you have 9–12 months of hands-on IT experience and are targeting networking roles

CompTIA A+ vs Network+: Quick Comparison

According to Pearson VUE’s 2025 Value of IT Certification Report, surveying nearly 24,000 IT professionals globally, 32% of certified candidates received a salary increase after earning a certification, and 31% of those raises exceeded 20%. Here’s how A+ and Network+ compare side by side:

LevelEntry-level, vendor-neutralEntry-level, vendor-neutral
Number of ExamsTwo (Core 1 + Core 2)One
Exam Cost~$246 per exam (~$492 total)$369 USD
Questions per ExamUp to 90 per examUp to 90
Duration90 minutes per exam90 minutes
Passing Score675/900 (Core 1), 700/900 (Core 2)720/900
Avg. Salary Range$54K–$64K/yr$74K–$82K/yr
Pass Rate (est.)~70–80%~70–75%
Study Time80–160 hours100–280 hours
Recommended ExperienceNone requiredA+ or 9–12 months networking experience
RenewalEvery 3 years (20 CEUs)Every 3 years (30 CEUs)
Best ForHelp desk, desktop support, IT support techNetwork admin, junior network engineer, NOC tech

CompTIA A+ vs Network+: Salary Data

According to ZipRecruiter, the average annual pay for a CompTIA A+ certified professional in the United States is $63,909 as of April 2026. Network+ holders fare better: Training Camp’s 2025 salary analysis puts the average Network+ salary at $81,643, with a 20% premium over non-certified peers.

The ~$18K salary gap reflects the difference in scope. Network+ is a depth credential in a specific technical domain. A+ is broad by design — it touches hardware, operating systems, networking basics, security, and troubleshooting across a wide range of scenarios. That breadth opens more entry points but typically at lower starting pay.

One important caveat: many professionals hold both. A help desk technician who earns A+ and then adds Network+ within 12–18 months can transition into network support roles with a substantial pay increase. The certifications are complementary, not competing.

CompTIA A+ Exam: What It Actually Tests

The CompTIA A+ certification (version 15, released March 2025) requires passing two separate exams. It is the only CompTIA certification with a two-exam requirement, which is worth factoring into your budget and timeline. At ~$246 per exam, passing both costs roughly $492 in exam fees alone — before accounting for study materials.

A+ Core 1 (220-1201) Domains

  • Mobile Devices — laptops, mobile hardware, ports and connectors
  • Networking — TCP/IP, wireless, SOHO networking, internet connection types
  • Hardware — cables, connectors, RAM, storage devices, power supplies, printers
  • Virtualization and Cloud Computing — cloud models, hypervisors, virtual networking
  • Hardware and Network Troubleshooting — systematic troubleshooting methodology

A+ Core 2 (220-1202) Domains

  • Operating Systems — Windows, macOS, Linux, ChromeOS installation and management
  • Security — malware removal, endpoint hardening, mobile device management
  • Software Troubleshooting — application errors, OS problems, scripting basics
  • Operational Procedures — documentation, change management, incident response, safety

The A+ exam is broad by design. CompTIA describes it as validating foundational IT skills across hardware, software, and basic security. If you work a help desk role where you’ll handle everything from replacing RAM to removing ransomware to setting up printers, A+ maps directly to the job. You can use our free Security+ practice exam to benchmark your current knowledge and see how much security overlap you already have before committing to a study plan.

CompTIA Network+ Exam: What It Actually Tests

CompTIA recommends that candidates hold CompTIA A+ certification (or have equivalent experience) before sitting Network+. The exam is a single test — up to 90 questions in 90 minutes — with a passing score of 720 on a 100–900 scale. Study time estimates range from 100 hours for candidates with some networking exposure to 280 hours for complete beginners (CompTIA, 2025).

Network+ (N10-009) Domains

  • Networking Concepts (23%) — OSI model, protocols, ports, cloud networking, subnetting
  • Network Implementation (19%) — routing, switching, VLANs, wireless standards
  • Network Operations (17%) — monitoring, documentation, backup, disaster recovery
  • Network Security (20%) — threats, attacks, hardening, authentication, VPN
  • Network Troubleshooting (21%) — troubleshooting methodology, tools, wired and wireless issues

The troubleshooting domain (21%) is where preparation most often determines whether candidates pass or fail. Unlike hardware troubleshooting in A+, Network+ troubleshooting scenarios involve diagnosing connectivity issues between devices across subnets, identifying routing table problems, and tracing down wireless interference — skills that are hard to develop without lab practice. If you have a set of Network+ practice questions, our free file upload simulator lets you run them in your browser without any software installation.

Which Exam Is Harder?

Both A+ and Network+ carry estimated first-attempt pass rates of around 70–80%, according to informal surveys and training center reports — CompTIA does not publish official pass rates. For context, Cisco CCNA sits at a lower ~50–60% pass rate, making both CompTIA entry-level credentials significantly more accessible. See our Network+ vs CCNA comparison for a detailed breakdown of that gap.

In terms of raw difficulty perception:

  • A+ feels harder to study for because the content breadth is enormous — you’re covering hardware, operating systems, networking basics, mobile devices, security, and operational procedures across two separate 90-question exams. Beginners report feeling overwhelmed by the volume of material.
  • Network+ feels harder conceptually because subnetting, routing protocols, and packet analysis require deeper logical reasoning than memorizing hardware components. Candidates who rush past the fundamentals consistently struggle on performance-based questions.

A+ is more forgiving if you have real-world IT support experience. Network+ rewards candidates who have touched actual network equipment — even virtually through Packet Tracer or GNS3 — far more than those who studied purely from books.

Job Market: Which Certification Opens More Doors?

The Bureau of Labor Statistics projects demand for computer support specialists to grow 6% from 2023 to 2033 — faster than the national average for most occupations (BLS, 2024). That growth underpins demand for both certifications, but in different job categories.

Jobs Requiring or Preferring CompTIA A+

  • Help Desk Technician / IT Support Specialist
  • Desktop Support Technician
  • Field Service Technician
  • IT Technician (hardware repair and deployment)
  • End User Computing Technician

Entry-level help desk technicians with A+ earn a median $52,000–$56,500, with experienced roles pushing above $64,000. Many government agencies and DoD contractors specifically require CompTIA A+ as a baseline credential — it appears in the DoD 8570/8140 compliance framework, making it a compliance-driven hire in defense and government IT.

Jobs Requiring or Preferring CompTIA Network+

  • Network Technician / Network Support Technician
  • Junior Network Administrator
  • NOC (Network Operations Center) Technician
  • Systems Administrator (networking component)
  • IT Infrastructure Technician

Glassdoor shows over 6,573 U.S. job listings seeking Network+ certification, with competitive salaries typically in the $83,000–$139,000 range for specialized networking roles. At the entry level (junior network admin, NOC tech), salaries start around $50,000–$65,000 and scale quickly with experience.

Which Should You Get First?

The right answer depends on three factors: your current experience level, the specific roles you’re targeting, and how much study time you can commit.

Get CompTIA A+ First If:

  • You have little to no IT background — A+ builds foundational knowledge across hardware, software, and basic networking that makes Network+ content easier to absorb later
  • You’re targeting help desk, desktop support, or IT support technician roles as your entry point into IT
  • You want the credential with the broadest entry-level employer recognition — A+ appears in the most entry-level IT job listings of any certification
  • You’re working toward government or defense IT roles where DoD 8570/8140 compliance is a factor
  • You want to follow the path CompTIA itself recommends before attempting Network+

Get CompTIA Network+ First If:

  • You already have 9–12 months of hands-on IT experience — you know how to troubleshoot basic hardware and software issues and are ready to specialize
  • You’re targeting networking-specific roles rather than general IT support
  • You want a single-exam credential (vs. A+’s two exams) to get certified faster and at lower initial cost ($369 vs. ~$492)
  • You plan to eventually pursue Cisco CCNA, as Network+ provides strong conceptual grounding for that path
  • You already have equivalent foundational knowledge from a bootcamp, degree program, or self-study

The Case for Getting Both

Many employers posting entry-level network administration roles list both A+ and Network+ as preferred credentials. Holding both signals foundational breadth (hardware, OS, support procedures) plus networking depth. The total cost for both — approximately $861 in exam fees — is still far less than a semester of community college and can be completed in 6–12 months of self-study. Our guide to active recall and spaced repetition study methods covers how to structure a multi-certification preparation schedule efficiently.

Free Study Resources for A+ and Network+

You do not need to spend money on expensive study materials to pass either exam. Here are the most effective free resources:

For CompTIA A+

  • Professor Messer’s free A+ course (professormesser.com) — comprehensive video coverage mapped to the current exam objectives, completely free
  • ExamCompass free A+ practice tests — domain-specific question banks with no signup required
  • UnionTestPrep A+ study guide — free text-based guides covering all exam domains
  • CertQuiz file upload — if you have A+ practice questions in VCE, PDF, or DOCX format, upload them here and run them as an interactive quiz in your browser

For CompTIA Network+

  • Professor Messer’s free Network+ course — free video series covering N10-009 objectives
  • Cisco Packet Tracer (free) — network simulation software; subnetting and routing hands-on practice is essential for the troubleshooting domain
  • Study-CCNA.com — free networking tutorials; the subnetting and TCP/IP sections are directly applicable to Network+ content
  • CertQuiz file upload — upload your Network+ practice questions in any format and practice them as an interactive quiz

For both exams, the most effective single study activity is practice testing under timed conditions. Candidates who incorporate structured practice testing pass at significantly higher rates than those who rely on reading and video alone. Our study methods guide explains the research behind this in detail.

Cost Breakdown: A+ vs Network+

Exam cost is a real factor for many candidates, especially those self-funding their certification path. Here is an honest total cost comparison:

Cost ItemCompTIA A+CompTIA Network+
Exam Voucher(s)~$246 x 2 = ~$492$369
Retake Risk (if failing once)+$246 per failed exam+$369
Free Study MaterialsProfessor Messer, ExamCompassProfessor Messer, Packet Tracer
Optional Paid Study Book$30–$60 (Mike Meyers / Mike Chapple)$30–$55 (Mike Meyers / Darril Gibson)
Total (first attempt, free study)~$492~$369
Total (if one retake needed)~$738~$738

Network+ has a lower initial exam cost and requires only one voucher. A+ carries higher upfront exam fees but has the broader entry-level job applicability. If cost is a constraint, starting with Network+ (if you have the prerequisite experience) is financially efficient. If you need to build foundational skills first, A+ is the investment that pays off by making everything after it easier.

Career Path: Where Does Each Cert Lead?

Think of A+ and Network+ as the first two rungs on separate but connected ladders. The Security+ certification sits above both as the natural next step for security-focused careers.

Typical A+ Career Path

Help Desk Technician → Desktop Support → IT Support Specialist → Systems Administrator → (Security+) → Security Analyst

Typical Network+ Career Path

NOC Technician / Junior Network Admin → Network Administrator → (CCNA) → Network Engineer → Senior Network Architect

Both paths converge at the systems and security levels. Many network administrators eventually add Security+ to move into security engineering roles, and many security analysts add Network+ to strengthen their infrastructure fundamentals. If you’re planning the security route, our Security+ vs CySA+ guide covers what comes after Security+.

FAQ

Can I skip A+ and go straight to Network+?

Yes — Network+ has no formal prerequisites. CompTIA recommends A+ or 9–12 months of hands-on experience, but this is guidance, not a requirement. If you already understand basic hardware, operating systems, and can troubleshoot common user issues from work experience or self-study, skipping A+ is a reasonable time and cost decision. About 20–25% of Network+ content (especially the networking fundamentals and hardware domains) overlaps with A+ material. Candidates who skipped A+ often underestimate how much foundational context it provides.

Which certification is more recognized by employers?

A+ has broader name recognition at the entry level. It appears in more help desk and IT support job listings than any other certification. Network+ has stronger recognition in networking-specific job listings and is widely accepted across government and military IT roles under DoD 8570/8140. Both are CompTIA credentials with strong industry acceptance — neither is obscure or questioned by technical hiring managers. According to Pearson VUE’s 2025 report, 82% of certified professionals gained confidence to pursue new job opportunities after earning their certification.

How long does it take to prepare for each exam?

For A+: plan for 80–160 hours over 6–10 weeks for a complete beginner. Candidates with some IT background can prepare in 4–6 weeks. For Network+: plan for 100–200 hours over 8–12 weeks without networking experience. Candidates with hands-on experience can often prepare in 4–6 weeks. The most effective approach for either exam is daily practice testing combined with spaced repetition review of weak domains. Our study method guide covers a 6-week preparation template you can adapt for either cert.

Is A+ still worth it in 2026?

Yes, especially for career changers entering IT for the first time. The BLS projects 6% growth in computer support specialist roles through 2033, and help desk positions remain one of the most accessible IT entry points with no prior degree required. A+ is recognized in the DoD 8570/8140 framework, making it a compliance requirement in defense and government IT — a segment of the market that actively hires A+ holders. The median total pay for help desk technicians reached $64,000 as of late 2025, and many A+ holders add Network+ or Security+ within 12–18 months to move into higher-paying specializations.

Should I get A+ before Security+?

CompTIA recommends Network+ before Security+, with A+ as the step before Network+. That said, many candidates successfully pass Security+ without holding A+ — Security+ itself has no prerequisites. If your goal is a cybersecurity role and you have some networking and OS background from other experience, you can go directly to Security+. title: How to Study for IT Certification Exams: Active Recall and Spaced Repetition Methods That Work (2026)
description: Learn how to study for IT certification exams using active recall and spaced repetition — science-backed methods that double retention and improve first-attempt pass rates for CompTIA, AWS, Azure, and Cisco.
author: CertQuiz Team
content:
Most people preparing for IT certification exams study the wrong way. They re-read notes, watch video courses on loop, and then wonder why they blank out on exam day. The problem isn't effort — it's method. Research shows that students using active recall remember around 57% of material, compared to just 29% retention with passive reading (FlashGenius, 2024). Switching how you study for IT certification exams can be the difference between passing on your first attempt and burning months of evenings for nothing.

This guide covers the two methods backed by decades of cognitive science research — active recall and spaced repetition — and shows you exactly how to apply them to CompTIA, AWS, Azure, and Cisco exam prep. Everything here is free. Use our free Security+ practice exam to start applying these techniques right now, no account required.

Key Takeaways

  • Active recall produces roughly double the retention of passive re-reading, according to Roediger and Karpicke's foundational research at Washington University
  • Without spaced review, people forget up to 70% of new material within 24 hours (Ebbinghaus forgetting curve)
  • The Security+ SY0-701 first-attempt pass rate is estimated at 50–65% for self-study and rises to 85–93% with structured, practice-heavy preparation
  • 32% of IT professionals who earned a new certification received a direct salary increase, and 56% saw that raise within three months (Pearson VUE 2025 Value of IT Certification Report)
  • Practice tests outperform video-only study: candidates who incorporated structured practice testing were significantly more likely to pass on their first attempt

Why Most IT Certification Study Plans Fail

According to the Ebbinghaus forgetting curve — one of the most replicated findings in psychology — people forget up to 70% of newly learned information within 24 hours without deliberate review, and retain only about 25% by the end of the week (PMC Replication of Ebbinghaus Forgetting Curve, 2015). If your study routine involves watching a four-hour video block and then moving on, you are fighting your own memory.

The most common mistakes candidates make when studying for IT certifications:

  • Passive re-reading — going through the same notes or book chapters repeatedly creates an illusion of mastery without actually building recall
  • Massed practice (cramming) — studying the same material in one long session, then never returning to it
  • Skipping wrong answers — reviewing only questions you got right reinforces confidence, not knowledge gaps
  • No timed simulation — never practicing under exam conditions means time pressure becomes a major variable on test day
  • Topic sequencing errors — studying exam domains in isolation rather than mixing them, which reduces your ability to connect concepts

Each of these failure modes has a direct counter in the active recall and spaced repetition framework described below.

Active Recall: The Core of Effective IT Certification Study

Roediger and Karpicke's landmark 2006 research at Washington University found that practicing retrieval just one time doubled long-term retention compared to re-studying the same material. Repeated retrieval produced a 400% improvement in retention relative to passive study (Roediger & Karpicke, 2006). This is the testing effect — and it is the foundation of every high-performance certification study plan.

Active recall means forcing your brain to retrieve information from memory, rather than simply recognizing it on a page. The act of retrieval itself strengthens the neural pathway. Recognition (seeing an answer and thinking "yes, I knew that") does almost nothing for long-term memory. Retrieval does.

Active Recall Techniques for IT Exam Prep

1. Practice questions first, not last. Most candidates watch videos or read chapters, then use practice questions to "check" understanding at the end. Flip this. Start a study session with 15–20 practice questions on the topic before you review material. This primes your brain to notice what it doesn't know, and the subsequent reading sticks far better. Our free Security+ practice exam lets you run focused domain sessions — start with your weakest domain, not your strongest.

2. Closed-book answer reconstruction. After reading a section or watching a segment, close everything and write down every concept, term, and connection you can remember. Don't look back until you've exhausted your memory. Then compare. The gap between what you wrote and what you missed is your actual study target.

3. Scenario-based flashcards. Standard flashcards test definitions. Certification exams test application. Write flashcards as scenarios: "A user reports their browser is redirecting to unfamiliar sites after visiting a PDF link. What attack type is this? What response steps apply?" This mirrors how Security+, Network+, and AWS exams actually phrase questions.

4. Teach it out loud. Explaining a concept aloud — to yourself, a study partner, or even a phone recording — forces retrieval and exposes gaps immediately. If you can't explain what a subnet mask does in 60 seconds without looking at notes, you don't know it well enough for exam day.

5. Answer every question before reading the explanation. When working through practice exams, always commit to an answer before revealing the explanation. Candidates who read explanations without committing first develop pattern recognition for answer choices rather than true understanding of concepts.

Spaced Repetition: How to Study for IT Certification Exams Over Time

A 2025 meta-analysis of 22 classroom studies with over 3,000 participants found a consistent moderate effect in favor of distributed (spaced) practice over massed practice, with an effect size of d = 0.54 (PMC Distributed Practice Meta-Analysis, 2025). The finding spans more than a century of research — but it is routinely ignored by people under time pressure who feel like cramming is their only option.

Spaced repetition means reviewing material at increasing intervals. The first review should happen within 24 hours of initial learning, the second after three days, the third after seven days, and so on. Each successful retrieval pushes the next review interval further out. Failed retrievals reset the interval. Over time, this approach builds genuinely durable memory rather than short-term familiarity.

Building a Spaced Repetition Schedule for Your Certification

Here is a practical schedule for a 6-week Security+ or AWS CCP preparation window using spaced repetition principles:

WeekDaily FocusReview ObligationPractice Tests
Week 1Domain 1 content (new material)Review Day 1 material on Day 210–15 Domain 1 questions daily
Week 2Domain 2 content (new material)Review Week 1 material on Day 1010–15 Domain 2 + 5 Domain 1 daily
Week 3Domain 3 content (new material)Review Weeks 1–2 material at midpointMixed domain 25-question sessions
Week 4Domain 4–5 content (new material)Review all prior domains onceFull 90-question timed simulation
Week 5Gap review (weak areas only)Second pass on all domainsTwo full timed simulations
Week 6Light review + restQuick-fire flashcards on weak spotsOne final full simulation, no cramming last 48hr

You can adapt this schedule to any exam. The core rule: every topic you study should be revisited at least three times before your exam date, with increasing intervals between each review.

Using Anki for IT Certification Flashcards

Anki is the most widely used spaced repetition software, and the research on its effectiveness is extensive. A 2023 cohort study found that high-frequency Anki users outperformed minimal users on standardized exams by 4–13 points, with a dose-response relationship — more consistent daily use produced better outcomes (PMC Anki Cohort Study, 2023).

For IT certification prep, the most effective Anki approach is:

  • Create scenario-based cards, not definition-only cards ("What does ARP do?" is weak; "Why would you see unexpected ARP replies on a network segment?" is stronger)
  • Keep each card to a single concept — one question, one answer
  • Do your daily Anki reviews before new study content, not after (you're fresher for retrieval early)
  • Rate cards honestly — if you hesitated or got it partially wrong, mark it as incorrect so the interval resets
  • Target 20–30 new cards per day maximum; clearing 100+ overdue cards is more important than adding new ones

If you prefer not to build cards from scratch, you can upload your existing practice question files to our free simulator — VCE, PDF, and DOCX formats all work — and use them as your active recall source.

Applying These Methods to Specific Certifications

CompTIA Security+ (SY0-701)

Security+ is the most widely held entry-level cybersecurity certification. A 2024 Skillsoft survey of 1,905 CompTIA-certified professionals found that 62% hold Security+. The exam has up to 90 questions in 90 minutes, with a significant portion being performance-based questions (PBQs) that require applied thinking, not just recall.

Active recall is especially important for Security+ because PBQs cannot be memorized — they require you to apply knowledge to simulated scenarios. The best preparation strategy:

  • Use our free SY0-701 practice test to identify weak domains before starting structured review
  • Build scenario-based Anki cards for every attack type, protocol, and framework in the exam objectives
  • Practice PBQ-style questions separately — they take 3–5x longer per question and should not be left until the end of your timed simulation
  • Review our CompTIA Security+ study guide for domain-by-domain coverage

AWS Cloud Practitioner (CLF-C02)

The AWS Cloud Practitioner exam is 65 questions over 90 minutes and focuses on cloud concepts, core services, security, and pricing. Because the content is conceptual rather than deeply technical, passive reading feels effective — but it isn't. Candidates who rely on reading the AWS whitepaper and watching video courses without active self-testing routinely underestimate the specificity of exam questions.

  • Build flashcards for every AWS service acronym and its primary use case — the exam tests precise service selection
  • Practice "when to use which service" scenarios: "A company needs object storage for infrequently accessed data. Which S3 storage class applies?"
  • Read our AWS CCP vs AZ-900 comparison to understand which cert fits your path before committing study hours

CompTIA Network+ (N10-009)

Network+ covers networking concepts, infrastructure, operations, security, and troubleshooting. The troubleshooting domain (22% of the exam) is where spaced repetition pays off most — there are dozens of distinct troubleshooting scenarios and the differences between them are subtle enough that massed study produces confusion, not retention.

  • Create "symptom to cause to fix" flashcard chains: front of card shows the symptom, back shows the likely cause and the resolution step
  • Review our Network+ vs CCNA comparison if you're deciding between them
  • Space your troubleshooting scenario practice across the full study window — don't batch it in the final week

How to Measure Whether Your Study Methods Are Working

The most reliable signal is your practice test performance trend over time, not any single score. You should be tracking:
